# The For-Sale Market {#sec-market-ownership}

<!-- Purpose: ownership-market dynamics — prices, payments, inventory, and buyer affordability for the study area (PLAN.md §7 Ch 3a).
     Narrative: prose migrated from the team's Google Doc draft (Oct 2026); numbers audited against the data. -->

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")

mls  <- read_rds("data/mls.rds")
fred <- read_rds("data/fred.rds")
gaps <- read_rds("data/gaps.rds")
inc  <- read_rds("data/acs_income.rds")

# Palette anchors (match ggtext subtitle spans to line/fill colors)
blue   <- hda_pal[1]
green  <- hda_pal[2]
yellow <- hda_pal[3]
coral  <- hda_pal[4]

# CPI deflator to the latest full year (2026 CPI is still NA) — real dollars = base-year dollars
cpi_base_year <- max(fred$cpi$year[!is.na(fred$cpi$cpi_less_shelter)])
cpi_base      <- fred$cpi$cpi_less_shelter[fred$cpi$year == cpi_base_year]

# Monthly principal-and-interest on the median home (10% down, 30-yr fixed) — reused by F3
mortgage_pi <- function(price, annual_rate_pct, down = 0.10, n = 360) {
  loan <- price * (1 - down)
  r <- annual_rate_pct / 100 / 12
  loan * r * (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
}

# --- Inline scalars for bullet text -------------------------------------------
ann <- mls$annual
med_2025    <- ann$median_price[ann$year == 2025]                       # 650000
peak_yr     <- ann$year[ann$year <= 2025][which.max(ann$sales_count[ann$year <= 2025])]  # 2021
peak_sales  <- max(ann$sales_count[ann$year <= 2025])                   # 1466
sales_2025  <- ann$sales_count[ann$year == 2025]                        # 938
sales_decline <- 1 - sales_2025 / peak_sales                            # ~0.36

# Real (base-year $) county price, 2016 vs 2025
p16      <- ann$median_price[ann$year == 2016]
cpi16    <- fred$cpi$cpi_less_shelter[fred$cpi$year == 2016]
p16_real <- p16 * cpi_base / cpi16

# Price / payment / income growth (2016 base) — indices built in F3 chunk
idx_price_2025 <- med_2025 / p16 * 100
pay16 <- mortgage_pi(p16, fred$pmms_annual$mortgage_rate_30yr[fred$pmms_annual$year == 2016])
pay25 <- mortgage_pi(med_2025, fred$pmms_annual$mortgage_rate_30yr[fred$pmms_annual$year == 2025])
idx_pay_2025 <- pay25 / pay16 * 100
inc16 <- inc$b19013_trend$estimate[inc$b19013_trend$GEOID == fauquier & inc$b19013_trend$year == 2016]
inc24 <- inc$b19013_trend$estimate[inc$b19013_trend$GEOID == fauquier & inc$b19013_trend$year == 2024]
idx_inc_2024 <- inc24 / inc16 * 100

# F6 affordability — reused from gaps.rds (NOT recomputed)
buyer_income  <- gaps$income_needed$buyer_income   # 204891 (7.33% PMMS, Oct 2026)
med_price     <- gaps$income_needed$med_price      # 650000
actual_income <- inc24                             # 130189 (Fauquier 2024 median HH income)
income_gap    <- buyer_income - actual_income      # ~74702

# F5 / F7 snapshot scalars (single for-sale active-listing snapshot, transaction export;
# rental listings are split out in mls$active_rentals)
active_n    <- nrow(mls$active)                                   # export subset, not the published count
active_u350 <- sum(mls$active$list_price < 350000, na.rm = TRUE)
active_asof <- format(max(mls$active$snapshot_date), "%B %Y")     # month of the snapshot

# 2026 year-to-date vs the same months of 2025 (2026 is a partial year)
ytd_last_m  <- max(mls$monthly$month[mls$monthly$year == 2026])
ytd_26      <- sum(mls$monthly$sales_count[mls$monthly$year == 2026])
ytd_25      <- sum(mls$monthly$sales_count[mls$monthly$year == 2025 & mls$monthly$month <= ytd_last_m])
ytd_chg     <- ytd_26 / ytd_25 - 1
ytd_thru    <- month.name[ytd_last_m]

# --- Monthly Bright MLS published summary (2022+, by geography) — F5 supply & DOM ------
ms     <- mls$monthly_summary
ms_fau <- ms |> filter(geography == "Fauquier")
sup_yr <- ms_fau |> summarize(active = mean(active_listings), mos = mean(months_supply), .by = year)
active_avg_2022 <- round(sup_yr$active[sup_yr$year == 2022])
active_avg_2025 <- round(sup_yr$active[sup_yr$year == 2025])
active_avg_2026 <- round(sup_yr$active[sup_yr$year == 2026])     # 2026 = year to date
mos_avg_2022    <- sup_yr$mos[sup_yr$year == 2022]
mos_avg_2025    <- sup_yr$mos[sup_yr$year == 2025]
mos_avg_2026    <- sup_yr$mos[sup_yr$year == 2026]
latest_ms       <- ms_fau |> slice_max(date, n = 1)              # latest published month (Oct = partial)
active_pub_now  <- latest_ms$active_listings
mos_pub_now     <- latest_ms$months_supply
latest_ms_lbl   <- format(latest_ms$date, "%B %Y")
active_pub_yago <- ms_fau$active_listings[ms_fau$date == latest_ms$date - years(1)]   # same month, prior year

# Reconciliation: Bright MLS published sales counts run consistently above the
# transaction-export counts that drive the annual series (systematic ~17–23% level offset;
# median price agrees to ~0.1%). Same filter affects the active-listing snapshot. See callout.
# Volume is NOT re-based on either source.
sales_pub_2025 <- sum(ms_fau$sales_n[ms_fau$year == 2025])
sales_gap_pct  <- sales_pub_2025 / sales_2025 - 1

# Town-boundary prices (Bright MLS published town statistics): annual sales-weighted average of
# monthly medians, 2022+ (2026 = year to date). ZIP-based medians (mls$annual_zip) are context only.
town_px <- ms |>
  filter(geography != "Fauquier", sales_n > 0) |>
  summarize(median_price = weighted.mean(median_price, sales_n), sales = sum(sales_n),
            .by = c(geography, year)) |>
  rename(town = geography)
tp  <- \(t, y) town_px$median_price[town_px$town == t & town_px$year == y]
zp  <- \(t, y) mls$annual_zip$median_price[mls$annual_zip$town == t & mls$annual_zip$year == y]
med_2026 <- ann$median_price[ann$year == 2026]
# Town months of supply: average listings ÷ average monthly sales (robust to thin-sales months)
town_mos     <- \(t, y) with(ms[ms$geography == t & ms$year == y, ], mean(active_listings) / mean(sales_n))
town_sales   <- \(t, y) mean(ms$sales_n[ms$geography == t & ms$year == y])
town_active  <- \(t, y) mean(ms$active_listings[ms$geography == t & ms$year == y])
bea_mos_2026 <- town_mos("Bealeton", 2026)

# Mortgage rate: latest month, and the last month that was higher
rate_now      <- fred$pmms_monthly |> filter(!is.na(mortgage_rate_30yr)) |> slice_max(date, n = 1)
rate_prev_hi  <- fred$pmms_monthly |> filter(date < rate_now$date, mortgage_rate_30yr >= rate_now$mortgage_rate_30yr) |>
  slice_max(date, n = 1)

# Active for-sale snapshot profile
act <- mls$active |> filter(!is.na(list_price), list_price > 0)
act_med      <- median(act$list_price)
act_750      <- mean(act$list_price > 750000)
act_250_350  <- sum(act$list_price >= 250000 & act$list_price < 350000)
is_new       <- str_detect(act$new_resale, "^New")
act_new      <- mean(is_new, na.rm = TRUE)
act_new_med  <- median(act$list_price[is_new])
act_small    <- sum(act$number_bedrooms <= 2, na.rm = TRUE)
act_distress <- sum(act$owned_by %in% c("REO", "Corporate"))
```

## Sales volume

```{r}
#| label: fig-sales-volume
#| fig-cap: "Home sales cooled sharply from the 2020–21 peak"
#| fig-alt: !expr 'paste0("Column chart of Fauquier County annual home sales from 2016 to 2026. Volume climbs from about ", format(ann$sales_count[ann$year == 2016], big.mark = ","), " in 2016 to a 2020–21 peak near 1,450–1,470, then falls to roughly 850 to 1,000 sales a year in 2022–2025. Columns through 2021 come from the earlier GP/VAR series and 2022 onward from Bright MLS; the final 2026 column is a partial year-to-date count of ", format(ytd_26, big.mark = ","), " closings through ", ytd_thru, ".")'

vol <- ann |> mutate(partial = year == 2026)

ggplot(vol, aes(year, sales_count, fill = source, alpha = partial)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.78) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2021.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey55") +
  annotate("text", x = 2021.5, y = max(vol$sales_count) * 1.03,
           label = "GP/VAR  |  Bright MLS", size = 3, color = "grey45", hjust = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2026, y = ann$sales_count[ann$year == 2026] + 90,
           label = "2026\nYTD", size = 2.7, color = "grey45", lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(GP = green, MLS = blue), guide = "none") +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 1, `TRUE` = 0.45), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.08))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2016, 2026, 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Home sales cooled sharply from the 2020–21 peak",
    subtitle = "Closed home sales per year, Fauquier County — <span style='color:#8baeaa'>**GP/VAR (2016–2021)**</span> spliced to <span style='color:#445ca9'>**Bright MLS (2022–2026)**</span>",
    caption = mls_cap("2016–2026 (2026 partial-year)"), x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_markdown())
```

Sales peaked at `r format(peak_sales, big.mark = ",")` sold in `r peak_yr` and have since fallen to `r format(sales_2025, big.mark = ",")` in 2025 (down about `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(sales_decline)` from the pandemic-era high). The cooling reflects Fauquier's thin supply and higher financing costs, not falling demand, as prices kept climbing through the slowdown (@fig-price-trend).

Counts through 2021 come from the GP/VAR annual series and 2022 onward from Bright MLS; 2026 is a partial year-to-date count (January through `r ytd_thru`) and is not comparable to the full years. Against the same months of 2025 (`r format(ytd_25, big.mark = ",")` closings), 2026 volume is `r if (abs(ytd_chg) < 0.05) "roughly flat" else if (ytd_chg > 0) "up" else "down"` at `r format(ytd_26, big.mark = ",")` (`r sprintf("%+.0f", ytd_chg * 100)`%), so the decline has leveled off rather than continued.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A note on sales counts
Bright MLS's **published monthly summary** reports roughly **`r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(sales_gap_pct)` more sales** than the transaction-level export used for the volume series above (e.g. `r format(round(sales_pub_2025), big.mark = ",")` vs `r format(sales_2025, big.mark = ",")` closings in 2025) — a near-constant level offset across every year, consistent with a property-type filter on the export. **Median sale prices agree between the two sources to within ~0.1%**, so the price findings are unaffected; the level of sales counts (and the active-listing snapshot below) should be read as the export's narrower definition, while the year-over-year trend holds under either source.
:::

## Prices

```{r}
#| label: fig-price-trend
#| fig-cap: "Prices climbed steeply — and kept rising even after inflation"
#| fig-alt: !expr 'paste0("Line chart of Fauquier County median sold price from 2016 through ", ytd_thru, " 2026. The nominal monthly line rises from about $360,000 to about ", label_dollar(accuracy = 1000)(med_2026), " in 2026 to date; the inflation-adjusted line in 2025 dollars, which ends in 2025, rises more gently from about $465,000 to $650,000. Two annual town lines beginning in 2022 sit below the county: Warrenton near ", label_dollar(accuracy = 1000)(tp("Warrenton", 2026)), " and Bealeton near ", label_dollar(accuracy = 1000)(tp("Bealeton", 2026)), " in 2026 to date.")'

cpi_j <- fred$cpi |> select(year, cpi_less_shelter)

county_long <- mls$monthly |>
  left_join(cpi_j, by = "year") |>
  transmute(date,
            Nominal = median_price,
            `Real`  = median_price * cpi_base / cpi_less_shelter) |>   # NA after the last CPI year
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "series", values_to = "price") |>
  filter(!is.na(price))

town_a <- town_px |>
  mutate(date = make_date(year, 7L, 1L))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = county_long, aes(date, price, color = series, linewidth = series)) +
  geom_line(data = town_a, aes(date, median_price, group = town, color = town), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = town_a, aes(date, median_price, color = town), size = 1.6) +
  geom_text(data = filter(town_a, year == max(year)), aes(date, median_price, label = town, color = town),
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 40, size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Nominal = "grey70", `Real` = blue,
                                Warrenton = coral, Bealeton = yellow), guide = "none") +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(Nominal = 0.7, `Real` = 1.1), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"),
                     expand = expansion(c(0.02, 0.05))) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y",
               expand = expansion(c(0.02, 0.16))) +
  labs(
    title = "Prices climbed steeply — and kept rising even after inflation",
    subtitle = "Median sold price — county <span style='color:#8a8a8a'>**nominal**</span> vs <span style='color:#445ca9'>**real (2025 $)**</span><br>towns <span style='color:#e76f52'>**Warrenton**</span> / <span style='color:#e9ab3f'>**Bealeton**</span> (nominal, annual, 2022+; 2026 to date)",
    caption = paste0(mls_cap("2016–2026"), "<br>Town lines use Bright MLS town-area statistics. ", cpi_cap()), x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_markdown())
```

The county's median sold price nearly doubled in nominal terms: about $`r round(p16/1e3)`k in 2016 to $`r round(med_2025/1e3)`k in 2025, an `r round(idx_price_2025 - 100)`% increase. Even after inflation, real prices rose from roughly $`r round(p16_real/1e3)`k to $`r round(med_2025/1e3)`k in 2025 dollars, a `r round(med_2025/p16_real*100 - 100)`% increase in genuine appreciation, not just inflation. So far in 2026 (through `r ytd_thru`) the county median is $`r round(med_2026/1e3)`k.

Homes inside the two towns sell for less than the county as a whole. In 2026 to date, Warrenton's median runs about $`r round(tp("Warrenton", 2026)/1e3)`k and Bealeton's about $`r round(tp("Bealeton", 2026)/1e3)`k, against the county's $`r round(med_2026/1e3)`k; in 2025 the figures were about $`r round(tp("Warrenton", 2025)/1e3)`k and $`r round(tp("Bealeton", 2025)/1e3)`k. Bealeton's drop from 2025 to 2026 rests on about `r town_px$sales[town_px$town == "Bealeton" & town_px$year == 2026]` sales, so it may reflect the mix of homes sold rather than a real price decline.[^town-zips]

[^town-zips]: Town series begin in 2022 because the county's 2016–2021 monthly series is VAR (county-only). They come from Bright MLS's published town-area statistics (annual figures are sales-weighted averages of monthly medians). The ZIP codes that carry the town names cover far more ground: the Warrenton ZIPs (20186/20187) had a 2026 median near $`r round(zp("Warrenton", 2026)/1e3)`k and Bealeton's 22712 near $`r round(zp("Bealeton", 2026)/1e3)`k, because they take in large rural parcels well beyond the town limits.

## Prices vs. payments vs. incomes

```{r}
#| label: fig-price-payment-income
#| fig-cap: "Monthly mortgage payments have far outrun both prices and incomes"
#| fig-alt: "Indexed line chart set to 100 in 2016 for Fauquier County. The monthly mortgage payment line rises fastest, reaching about 250 by 2025; the median sold price line reaches about 180; and median household income rises most slowly to about 145 by 2024. The gap between payments and incomes widens sharply after 2021 as mortgage rates jump."

idx <- ann |>
  filter(year >= 2016, year <= 2025) |>
  select(year, price = median_price) |>
  left_join(fred$pmms_annual, by = "year") |>
  mutate(payment = mortgage_pi(price, mortgage_rate_30yr)) |>
  left_join(inc$b19013_trend |> filter(GEOID == fauquier) |> select(year, income = estimate),
            by = "year") |>
  transmute(year,
            Price               = price   / price[year == 2016]   * 100,
            `Monthly payment`   = payment / payment[year == 2016] * 100,
            Income              = income  / income[year == 2016]  * 100) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "series", values_to = "index") |>
  filter(!is.na(index))

lab_pts <- idx |> slice_max(year, by = series)

ggplot(idx, aes(year, index, color = series)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = lab_pts, aes(label = series), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.15,
            size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Price = blue, `Monthly payment` = coral, Income = green),
                     guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(c(0.02, 0.05))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2016, 2025, 3), expand = expansion(c(0.02, 0.22))) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly mortgage payments have far outrun both prices and incomes",
    subtitle = "Indexed to 2016 = 100 — median <span style='color:#445ca9'>**price**</span>, <span style='color:#e76f52'>**monthly payment**</span> (10% down, 30-yr), and median household <span style='color:#8baeaa'>**income**</span>",
    caption = paste0(mls_cap("2016–2025", through = FALSE), " ", pmms_cap(), " ", acs_cap("B19013")), x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_markdown())
```

Over 2016–2025 the median home sales price rose +`r round(idx_price_2025 - 100)`%, but the monthly payment on that home rose +`r round(idx_pay_2025 - 100)` percent. This is likely a reflection of the 30-year rate that climbed from `r sprintf("%.2f", fred$pmms_annual$mortgage_rate_30yr[fred$pmms_annual$year==2021])`% in 2021 to `r sprintf("%.2f", fred$pmms_annual$mortgage_rate_30yr[fred$pmms_annual$year==2025])`% in 2025, compounding the price increase. Rates have since climbed further, to `r sprintf("%.2f", rate_now$mortgage_rate_30yr)`% in `r format(rate_now$date, "%B %Y")`, the highest since `r format(rate_prev_hi$date, "%B %Y")`; at that rate the payment on the 2025 median home would be about $`r label_comma()(round(mortgage_pi(med_2025, rate_now$mortgage_rate_30yr), -1))` a month, versus $`r label_comma()(round(pay25, -1))` at the 2025 average. Median household income rose only +`r round(idx_inc_2024 - 100)`% through 2024, far behind both. Buying power has fallen sharply.[^gp-fig9]

[^gp-fig9]: The pattern matches the GP study's Figure 9 direction (GP: price +79%, payment +127%, income +35%); FHFH's actuals run somewhat higher on all three but tell the same story — payments ≫ prices ≫ incomes.

## Price segments

```{r}
#| label: fig-price-bands
#| fig-cap: "The entry-level segment has all but disappeared"
#| fig-alt: "Hundred-percent stacked column chart of Fauquier County home sales by price band from 2022 to 2026. The under-$250,000 band shrinks from about 4% to roughly 2%, and the $250,000–$350,000 band from about 10% to 4%, while the $500,000–$750,000 and $750,000-plus bands together grow to roughly three-quarters of all sales."

band_lvls <- c("<$250k", "$250-350k", "$350-500k", "$500-750k", "$750k+")
bands <- mls$sales_bands |>
  mutate(band = factor(band, levels = band_lvls))

sh <- \(y, b) bands$share[bands$year == y & bands$band == b]

ggplot(bands, aes(factor(year), share, fill = band)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.74) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_fill_hda() +
  labs(
    title = "The entry-level segment has all but disappeared",
    subtitle = "Share of closed home sales by price band, Fauquier County, 2022–2026 (2026 partial-year)",
    caption = paste0(mls_cap("2022–2026"),
                     " Earlier GP data show the under-$250k share falling from 27.8% (2016) to 3.0% (2021)."),
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda(flip_gridlines = FALSE) +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1))
```

Homes under $250k fell from `r label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(sh(2022, "<$250k"))` of sales in 2022 to `r label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(sh(2025, "<$250k"))` in 2025. Everything under $350k is now barely `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(sh(2025, "<$250k") + sh(2025, "$250-350k"))` of the market. As of the `r active_asof` listing snapshot, just `r active_u350` of `r active_n` active for-sale listings were priced under $350,000.

::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"}
Interviewees identified pricing as the most direct pressure on both housing and business: the county's stock skews toward high-end ownership, paired with aging but costly rentals. Realtors named starter and downsize homes (often the same unit) as the types missing from the market, and interviewees noted that in April 2026 just three homes were listed under $350,000.
:::

The $750k+ home price band has surged to `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(sh(2025, "$750k+"))` of sales from `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(sh(2022, "$750k+"))` in 2022. The modal band is now $500–750k (or `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(sh(2025, "$500-750k"))` of sales).

This is the tail end of a long collapse in the starter home market: the Greater Piedmont REALTOR's identified that under-$250k sales **fell from 27.8% in 2016 to 3.0% in 2021.** The MLS-only view here (2022+) shows the effective erosion of the market for entry level homes.

::: {.callout-note}
## What is listed for sale now
As of `r active_asof`, the median asking price across the `r active_n` active for-sale listings is **$`r label_comma()(act_med)`**, well above the $`r round(med_2026/1e3)`k median sale so far in 2026. `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(act_750)` of listings ask more than $750,000, and `r if (act_250_350 == 0) "none" else act_250_350` fall between $250,000 and $350,000. New construction makes up `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(act_new)` of listings at a median of $`r label_comma()(act_new_med)`. Only `r act_small` listings have two or fewer bedrooms. Bank-owned and corporate-owned listings number just `r act_distress`, so there is no sign of distressed sales. As with the rental snapshot (@sec-market-rental), this is a single day's inventory, so read it as directional.
:::

## Days on market & supply

```{r}
#| label: fig-days-on-market
#| fig-cap: "Homes still sell fast, but with a pronounced seasonal rhythm"
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of median days to sell for Fauquier County home sales, monthly from 2022 through October 2026. A faint monthly line swings between roughly 5 days in spring and 30 to 40 days in winter each year; a heavier three-month average line makes the seasonal sawtooth clear and drifts modestly higher in 2025 before easing in 2026."

roll3 <- \(x) as.numeric(stats::filter(x, rep(1/3, 3), sides = 2))

dom_m  <- ms_fau |> arrange(date) |> mutate(roll = roll3(days_to_sell))
dom_yr <- ms_fau |> summarize(dts = round(median(days_to_sell)), .by = year)
dg <- \(y) dom_yr$dts[dom_yr$year == y]

ggplot(dom_m, aes(date, days_to_sell)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey78", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = roll), color = blue, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, max(dom_m$days_to_sell) * 1.08), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y", expand = expansion(c(0.02, 0.04))) +
  labs(
    title = "Homes still sell fast, but with a pronounced seasonal rhythm",
    subtitle = "Median days to sell, Fauquier County — <span style='color:#b8b8b8'>**monthly**</span> and <span style='color:#445ca9'>**3-month average**</span>, 2022–2026",
    caption = mls_cap("2022–2026 (monthly summary)"), x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_markdown())
```

Despite the gap in availability of starter-style homes, the housing market (with larger single family homes) is still hot. Homes sell fast with a median `r dg(2022)` to `r dg(2024)` days on the market in 2022 - 2024. This rose to `r dg(2025)` days on the market in 2025, reflecting a cooling effect from increased rates. So far in 2026 (through `r ytd_thru`) the median is `r dg(2026)` days, little changed from 2025. This is still a matter of weeks, not months.

The monthly view exposes a strong seasonal rhythm that the annual averages can hide. Listings linger on the market for roughly 25 to 40 days in December through February and sell in under 10 days by spring yearly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-supply-trend
#| fig-cap: "Inventory has loosened from its pandemic lows — but supply is still tight"
#| fig-alt: !expr 'paste0("Two-panel chart for 2022 through ", ytd_thru, " 2026. The top panel shows active listings in Fauquier County rising from a 2022 low near 250 to a peak near 470 in spring 2026, then easing into fall, while Warrenton drifts up from the high 30s to about 50 and Bealeton roughly doubles from about 20 to about 40; the bottom panel shows months of supply climbing from about 3 to roughly 4 to 5 months for the county and Warrenton, while Bealeton''s smoothed line rises from about 2 to about ", round(bea_mos_2026), " months by 2026, with a brief late-2026 spike when sales dipped; all stay mostly below the dashed six-month line that marks a balanced market.")'

sup <- ms |>
  arrange(geography, date) |>
  transmute(geography, date,
            `Active listings`  = active_listings,
            `Months of supply` = months_supply) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(geography, date), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, levels = c("Active listings", "Months of supply")),
         roll = roll3(value), .by = c(geography, metric))

# Bealeton's thin monthly sales make its published months of supply swing wildly (one 2-sale month
# reads 21 months), so its smoothed line is 3-month listings ÷ 3-month sales and its raw line is omitted
bea_roll <- ms |> filter(geography == "Bealeton") |> arrange(date) |>
  transmute(date, bea = roll3(active_listings) / roll3(sales_n))
sup <- sup |>
  left_join(bea_roll, by = "date") |>
  mutate(roll  = if_else(geography == "Bealeton" & metric == "Months of supply", bea, roll),
         value = if_else(geography == "Bealeton" & metric == "Months of supply", NA_real_, value)) |>
  select(-bea)

thresh <- tibble(metric = factor("Months of supply",
                                 levels = levels(sup$metric)), yint = 6)

ggplot(sup, aes(date, value, color = geography)) +
  geom_hline(data = thresh, aes(yintercept = yint), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey55") +
  geom_line(aes(alpha = "raw"), linewidth = 0.4, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = roll, alpha = "roll"), linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Fauquier = blue, Warrenton = coral, Bealeton = yellow), guide = "none") +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(raw = 0.3, roll = 1), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(c(0, 0.08))) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y", expand = expansion(c(0.02, 0.04))) +
  labs(
    title = "Inventory has loosened from its pandemic lows — but supply is still tight",
    subtitle = "Active listings and months of supply (3-month average)<br><span style='color:#445ca9'>**Fauquier County**</span>, <span style='color:#e76f52'>**Warrenton**</span>, and <span style='color:#e9ab3f'>**Bealeton**</span>",
    caption = paste0(mls_cap("2022–2026 (monthly summary; October 2026 is a partial month)"),
                     "<br>Bealeton months of supply = 3-month listings ÷ 3-month sales; its monthly figures are too noisy to plot."), x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_markdown())
```

Active for-sale inventory has climbed from a tight `r format(active_avg_2022, big.mark = ",")` listings a month in 2022 to `r format(active_avg_2025, big.mark = ",")` in 2025 and `r format(active_avg_2026, big.mark = ",")` so far in 2026. There's a real loosening of the pandemic era squeeze with months of supply on the market - `r round(mos_avg_2022, 1)` to `r round(mos_avg_2025, 1)` months, and `r round(mos_avg_2026, 1)` in 2026. The latest published month (`r latest_ms_lbl`, data through `r mls_through`) shows `r active_pub_now` active listings and `r mos_pub_now` months of supply; active listings are `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(abs(active_pub_now / active_pub_yago - 1))` `r if (active_pub_now < active_pub_yago) "below" else "above"` a year earlier (`r active_pub_yago`), so the fall pullback is steeper than last year's.

Even so, supply stays well below the roughly six-month mark that separates a seller's from a buyer's market: Fauquier remains a seller's market, just a less extreme one than at the 2021–22 peak.

The towns are moving apart. Measured as average listings against average monthly sales, Warrenton holds about `r round(town_mos("Warrenton", 2026), 1)` months of supply in 2026, tighter than the county. Bealeton has loosened the most, from about `r round(town_mos("Bealeton", 2022), 1)` months in 2022 to about `r round(bea_mos_2026, 1)` in 2026: its active listings roughly doubled, from about `r round(town_active("Bealeton", 2022))` to `r round(town_active("Bealeton", 2026))`, while sales held near `r round(town_sales("Bealeton", 2026))` a month. Bealeton's small sales count makes its monthly figures swing widely, so the yearly averages are the better guide.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Inventory is recovering, not recovered
Contrary to a point-in-time reading, the monthly Bright MLS series shows active listings and months of supply trending upward since 2022 (from ~`r round(mos_avg_2022, 1)` months in 2022 to ~`r round(mos_avg_2025, 1)` in 2025 and ~`r round(mos_avg_2026, 1)` in 2026 to date), though the climb has flattened since 2025, as higher rates slowed the frantic pace. Fauquier is still firmly a **seller's market**, with supply short of the ~6-month balance point, and homes selling within weeks for most of the year.
:::

## What it takes to buy

```{r}
#| label: fig-income-to-buy
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Buying the median home takes about ", label_dollar()(round(income_gap, -3)), " more than the median household earns")'
#| fig-alt: !expr 'paste0("Two-bar comparison for Fauquier County. The income needed to afford the median-priced home is about ", label_dollar()(round(buyer_income, -2)), ", well above the actual median household income of about ", label_dollar()(round(actual_income, -2)), " — a gap of roughly ", label_dollar()(round(income_gap, -3)), ".")'

f6 <- tibble(
  what  = factor(c("Income needed to buy\nthe median home", "Actual median\nhousehold income"),
                 levels = c("Actual median\nhousehold income", "Income needed to buy\nthe median home")),
  value = c(buyer_income, actual_income),
  grp   = c("needed", "actual")
)

ggplot(f6, aes(value, what, fill = grp)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label_dollar(accuracy = 1000)(value)), hjust = -0.1,
            size = 3.4, color = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(needed = coral, actual = blue), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"),
                     expand = expansion(c(0, 0.18))) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Buying the median home takes about ", label_dollar()(round(income_gap, -3)), " more than the median household earns"),
    subtitle = paste0("Income required for the $", round(med_price / 1e3), "k median home vs. Fauquier's actual median household income"),
    caption = paste0("**Assumptions:** ", label_percent(accuracy = 0.01)(gaps$assumptions$mortgage_rate),
                     " 30-yr rate (PMMS, ", format(gaps$assumptions$rate_pull_date, "%b %Y"), "), ",
                     label_percent(accuracy = 1)(gaps$assumptions$down_payment), " down, ",
                     label_percent(accuracy = 1)(gaps$assumptions$front_end_ratio), " front-end ratio, $",
                     gaps$assumptions$tax_ins_monthly, "/mo taxes + insurance. ", acs_cap("B19013"),
                     " Parameters shared with the affordability-gaps analysis."),
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda(flip_gridlines = TRUE)
```

Homes available for sale in Fauquier are expensive relative to what local incomes can support. That said, both housing prices and incomes have risen in 10 years. However, affording the $`r round(med_price/1e3)`k median home requires about $`r format(round(buyer_income), big.mark = ",")` in household income under standard underwriting, versus Fauquier's actual $`r format(round(actual_income), big.mark = ",")` median, a gap of roughly $`r format(round(income_gap/1e3)*1e3, big.mark = ",")`. The gap is driven by the same forces as outlined in @fig-price-payment-income: high prices and a `r label_percent(accuracy = 0.01)(gaps$assumptions$mortgage_rate)` mortgage rate. The full owner/renter gap by income band is developed in @sec-gaps.

The squeeze is amplified by financing: monthly payments rose far faster than prices or incomes (@fig-price-payment-income).

As new construction skews larger and pricier (@sec-inventory), the sub-$350k segment has all but disappeared (@fig-price-bands), and the market still moves fast (@fig-days-on-market). This leaves entry-level buyers with few options at any quality level.

::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"}
Interviewees described a quality-versus-price mismatch for buyers: "what's affordable isn't desirable, and what's desirable isn't affordable." They said the resulting market works well for high-income commuters but squeezes the county's own workforce and tax base out of the picture.
:::
